operator.working_space: Oklab/OKLCh D65 with Ottosson matrices as published in NSEditing2

units.L: Oklab normalized 0 to 1, not Y or CIELAB L*
units.h: atan2(b,a) in degrees modulo 360. Increasing rotates red to yellow to green to cyan to blue to magenta.
units.delta_C_fraction: Signed fractional change from input C at full gate. +0.10 means 10 percent before blend.
units.a_b: signed Oklab axes. Positive a towards red, positive b towards yellow.
units.delta_Eok_x100: 100 times Euclidean distance in Cartesian Oklab. Engineering distance, no calibrated JND.

operator.tone_interpolation: PCHIP shape-preserving; same X and tangents as NSEditing2.curve/evaluate
operator.hue_interpolation: periodic pairwise raised cosine with half-cosine mix; append first knot +360
operator.gamut: NSEditing2.gamut(linear_sRGB, 0); common Rec.709 Y neutral axis. No compression before boundary. Last clamp for rounding.

PCHIP on L plus weighted hue-dependent delta_L
rotate h and multiply C using hue and L delta, attenuate positive chroma near sRGB boundary

encoded RGB lerp from original to full profile

M13.title: Photographic negatives may also suffer from degradation, especially color films. It is impossible to visualize the correct color of a color negative, as the orange or red appearance of the film is primarily a dye mask “filter” setting the appropriate color quality for the color print media it would eventually be printed to. Both this mask and the color dye layers in the film itself fade over time and are influenced by a variety of factors including exposure to heat and improper processing. The current practice of scanning the color negative, inverting the image, and color correcting the positive image does not produce an accurate representation of the original image as it would have looked if printed to photographic paper. Additionally, color negative films produced prior to 1975 (C22 process) do not scan well. Films produced after 1995 were designed to be scanned on the sophisticated digital photographic systems used just prior to the digital camera era.
